READING

**The numbers as stated**

VELLACOTT net outlay: 3,050,000 + 240,000 − 610,000 = GBP 2,680,000. Confirmed.
TARNSIDE total outlay: 1,420,000 + 310,000 = GBP 1,730,000. Confirmed.
Extra capital required for VELLACOTT over TARNSIDE: GBP 950,000.
Annual fuel saving under VELLACOTT: GBP 190,000.
Simple payback on that extra GBP 950,000: 950,000 ÷ 190,000 = **five years exactly**.

That single arithmetic result is the spine of this analysis. Within five years VELLACOTT has recovered the premium it costs over TARNSIDE purely from fuel. After year five it is generating GBP 190,000 per year in net savings on an ongoing basis, indefinitely, for as long as the Suilvenaig is in service. That is a strong financial argument before anything else is counted.

**Asset value over time**

TARNSIDE leaves you with a re-engined 1995 hull. By 2032, she is 37 years old. By 2036, 41. The hull survey passed cleanly in March 2026 and there is no structural problem today, but every survey cycle from here carries more risk, and surveyors' conditions on a hull that age will become progressively more restrictive. At some point — not necessarily far away — you will be back at this same decision, except the Brindlemere will be worth less than GBP 610,000 and a suitable replacement will cost more than the Suilvenaig costs today.

VELLACOTT gives you a 2017 hull. In 2032 she is 15 years old, comfortably in the middle of her working life. In 2036 she is 19. The capital tied up in her holds its value far better, and the next strategic horizon recedes by two decades. This is not captured in the simple five-year payback figure but it is real money.

**The charter and yard period**

TARNSIDE puts the Brindlemere in the yard for twelve weeks from 5 January 2027. That is mid-winter, which is the lighter-traffic half of the year (five crossings a day rather than eleven), so the timing is as good as it could be. The charter from Sorrelbank is agreed in principle at GBP 310,000 — a concrete number, not an estimate. Even so, operating a chartered vessel on your route for three months carries execution risk: familiarisation, crew preference, any unexpected delay in the yard extending the charter period. These risks are not large individually but they are real, and they are entirely absent under VELLACOTT.

**The crew question**

This is the most serious operational problem VELLACOTT carries. Losing two of nine masters is a 22% reduction in the rota. On a year-round single-vessel licence with eleven crossings a day in summer, seven masters is tight. The remaining seven each need a six-week course, which means that at any point during the training period one master is unavailable. If you run the training sequentially, you are looking at roughly 42 weeks of one-at-a-time absences — a long tail. Running two through the course concurrently halves that, but puts more pressure on the remaining active rota.

Three things reduce this concern, though they do not eliminate it. First, the two retiring masters may have been near the end of their working lives in any case; their departure may have been coming regardless of this decision. Second, the endorsement course exists, is completable in six weeks, and can in principle be offered to any suitably qualified master you recruit. Third — and this matters — you have time. The Suilvenaig can come over in November 2026. You can identify and begin training masters before the first full summer season on the new vessel. A careful plan, started now, can have enough endorsed masters in place before the high-season workload arrives.

TARNSIDE, by contrast, keeps all nine masters and changes nothing. That has genuine operational value. But it does not fix the rota problem forever; it simply defers it to the next vessel replacement.

**The insurance gap**

This is the one genuinely open variable that could, in theory, swing the decision. The broker has not quoted on the Suilvenaig. There is no figure to work with. In general, a 2017 hull attracts better hull-and-machinery terms than a 1995 hull; a newer vessel with a shorter claims history and modern safety systems is conventionally lower risk. Whether the endorsement requirement affects P&I or employer's liability terms is possible but not obviously large. On balance the insurance position is unlikely to be materially worse under VELLACOTT than under TARNSIDE, but it is not confirmed, and before the purchase contract is signed that quote must be in hand.

**Timing constraints**

The Kittiwake valuation of GBP 610,000 holds until 11 February 2027. The Suilvenaig handover is available from 20 November 2026. If Cormorant Sound commits to VELLACOTT now, there is roughly eleven weeks to complete the Suilvenaig transaction and roughly five and a half months to sell the Brindlemere within the valued figure. Neither window is comfortable but both are achievable. The Brindlemere is a known vessel with a valid hull survey and a long-standing maintenance record; she should be sellable within that period, especially to another operator in the island ferry sector. If the sale slips past 11 February, a fresh valuation would be needed, introducing uncertainty in both price and timing.

**What TARNSIDE actually delivers**

Re-engining resolves the one known mechanical deadline (engines and gearbox warranted only to end of 2027 summer season). It removes the crew and insurance unknowns. It avoids the linkspan spend. At GBP 1,730,000 it is substantially cheaper in year one. These are genuine advantages, not cosmetic ones.

But re-engining does not make the Brindlemere a different age. It does not reduce the fuel bill. It commits you to GBP 190,000 more fuel per year than the alternative, every year, until the Brindlemere is eventually replaced. And it does not solve the problem that she is a 1995 hull on an exposed year-round ferry route. TARNSIDE buys time — perhaps five to eight more years of service — at a cost that, when fuel is added year by year, catches up with VELLACOTT well within that period.

**Ten-year comparison (fuel only, ignoring residual value)**

TARNSIDE: GBP 1,730,000 capital + 10 × F fuel
VELLACOTT: GBP 2,680,000 capital + 10 × (F − 190,000) fuel
            = GBP 780,000 + 10 × F fuel

Over ten years, VELLACOTT costs GBP 950,000 less than TARNSIDE in capital plus fuel, before residual value, maintenance differentials, or any further capital event on the aging hull is counted. The residual value of a 2027-vintage Suilvenaig versus a 2027-vintage re-engined Brindlemere will widen that gap further.

**Conditions that should be met before executing VELLACOTT**

1. Get the insurance quote. If it materially exceeds current terms, revisit the arithmetic.
2. Establish a credible training schedule that gets enough masters endorsed before the first high season (May 2027).
3. Confirm the Brindlemere can be marketed immediately and that a realistic buyer pipeline exists within the valuation window.
4. Confirm the six-week course has sufficient availability to allow sequential or parallel scheduling across 2026–27.

None of these is a reason to choose TARNSIDE by default. All of them are actionable in the next four to six weeks.

**Overall**

TARNSIDE is the lower-risk choice in year one. VELLACOTT is the better choice over any horizon beyond five years, and operating a ferry licence on a year-round public route is a business measured in decades, not years. The crew challenge is real but manageable. The insurance question must be answered but is unlikely to close the gap. The financial case, the asset life case, and the avoidance of a yard period all point the same way.

CALL
  VELLACOTT

GROUNDS
  The GBP 190,000 annual fuel saving recovers the GBP 950,000 extra capital precisely at year five and generates net savings every year thereafter, while the Suilvenaig's 2017 hull carries residual value and remaining service life that a re-engined 1995 hull cannot match, making VELLACOTT the sounder investment over any planning horizon this business is actually managed to—provided the outstanding insurance quote is obtained before the purchase contract is signed.
